blocks.heading: Market and product orientation
blocks.text: Market orientation means research identifies customer wants before the product is developed and produced. Product orientation starts from the product or the enterprise’s technical strengths and then seeks buyers for that offering. The distinction is what guides the offering first, not whether either business advertises. Market focus can reduce the risk of an unwanted offer but costs time and research can be imperfect. Product focus can support technical innovation and expertise, yet may miss what buyers can use or afford. A business can combine technical capability with customer evidence rather than ignoring one.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Hela Bottles surveys users about size before designing a bottle. Another producer builds its preferred technical design first and then looks for buyers. Hela’s sequence is market oriented; the other is product led. Advertising after either decision does not change which information guided the design first.

blocks.heading: Market orientation
blocks.text: Market orientation is an approach in which market research finds consumer wants before the product is developed and produced. Customer evidence guides the offer, although the business must also assess cost and capability. Research may be inaccurate or needs may change, so continue to test the response.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ota Lunches asks workers about meal size and collection time before designing its menu. The customer findings lead the offering, so the sequence is market oriented.

blocks.heading: Product orientation
blocks.text: Product orientation starts from the product, technical capability or producer’s preferred design and seeks a market for it. It can support innovation and technical quality but risks producing something buyers do not want or cannot afford. It is not simply making a poor product or doing no promotion.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Hila Gear develops a technically preferred design, then looks for customers willing to buy it. The product leads the sequence. Advertising and later sales do not make the original design decision customer-research led.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain the orientation: Ula Bags asks customers about carrying problems before developing a range; Eha Cases designs its preferred case first and then seeks buyers.

Ula is market oriented because identified wants guide development. Eha is product oriented because its design focus precedes the search for buyers. Either may advertise later; the distinguishing fact is what guided the offering first.
